FIELD REFERENCE

Alligator gar: identification, size and Texas trip rules

Alligator gar (Atractosteus spatula), also called gator gar, have a short, broad snout and a heavy body covered in hard scales. Texas Parks and Wildlife describes fish over 300 pounds. For a Texas trip, check the exact water: harvest limits, spring closures and reporting rules can change what you may do.

Updated 2026-11-23 · Castward

How do you identify an alligator gar?

Key factDetail
Scientific nameAtractosteus spatula
Local nameGator gar
Size referenceTPWD species profile: up to 8 feet and over 300 pounds; not an expected catch
Alligator garBroad, short snout; heavy body
Longnose garMuch longer, narrower snout
Spotted garDark spots on head, body and fins
Shortnose garLacks the spotted gar’s dark marks on the head and paired fins
Texas statewide harvest1 daily; water-specific exceptions apply
Texas reportingReport harvest within 24 hours, except at Falcon International Reservoir

Alligator gar or longnose gar: what is the difference?

Compare the head from above. An alligator gar has a broad muzzle; a longnose gar has a narrow, drawn-out snout. Size alone is a poor test because longnose gar can also grow large. Juvenile alligator gar can resemble spotted gar, so compare several features before you identify the fish.

Read the source

When should you plan an alligator gar trip in Texas?

Spring travel needs a closure check. TPWD describes spawning in flooded vegetation, usually in April and May in Texas. That describes a biological season, not a promise of open fishing. Check the agency’s temporary-closure notice for your water before you set a date or choose a launch.

Read the source

Can you keep an alligator gar in Texas?

The statewide daily bag is one, with water-specific exceptions. Harvest from public waters must be reported within 24 hours, except at Falcon International Reservoir. Read the separate restrictions for your chosen water before keeping a fish. A statewide limit does not override a local closure or a special rule.

Read the source

Can a spring closure stop an alligator gar trip?

Yes. TPWD can close an area to taking or attempting to take alligator gar for up to 30 days when spawning conditions occur. The notice gives the affected area and reopening date. Check this before travel, and keep an alternative target or water in your trip plan.

Read the source

What should you know about alligator gar?

Is gator gar the same as alligator gar?

Yes. TPWD lists gator gar as another name for Atractosteus spatula.

Does a large gar have to be an alligator gar?

No. Longnose gar can also be large. Check the snout shape and body proportions.

Where do alligator gar live?

Their Gulf coastal range extends from Florida to Veracruz, Mexico. Texas records include large rivers, reservoirs and coastal bays.

Is spring always open for gar fishing?

No. Temporary spawning closures can apply to a named area. Read the current TPWD notice.

Do Texas anglers report released gar?

The cited mandatory report applies to harvested gar. Report harvest within 24 hours, except at Falcon International Reservoir.
